title: At the restaurant
topic: ordering and paying at a restaurant; tapas and the menú del día
why: After the market, it's restaurant time: the menú del día, tapas and raciones, and the phrases for ordering and paying, with usted introduced as the polite third-person form. The lesson recycles quantities and stem-changing verbs, and gives you the cultural landmarks (mealtimes, aperitivo, tipping) to eat like a Spaniard.

{"lessons": ["

The menú del día

At lunchtime on weekdays, almost every restaurant in Spain offers a menú del día: a full fixed-price meal (often between 12 and 16 euros). It includes:

SpanishEnglishExamples
el primero (de primero)the first course, the startergazpacho, ensalada mixta, sopa
el segundo (de segundo)the main coursemerluza, pollo asado, filete con patatas
el postre (de postre)dessertflan, fruta, arroz con leche
la bebidathe drinkagua, vino, una caña
el panbreadalways included

Ordering

To say what you'd like, use de primero, de segundo, de postre, and para mí (for me):

Para mí, de primero, el gazpacho, y de segundo, la merluza.For me, the gazpacho to start, and the hake for the main course.
¿Y para beber? Una botella de agua sin gas, por favor.And to drink? A bottle of still water, please.

Careful: don't translate the “for” in “for the main course” or “for dessert”: it's always de primero and so on, never “para primero.” And para mí takes an accent (the pronoun “me”), unlike mi (my).

The English word “menu” (the list of dishes) is la carta. El menú is the fixed-price set meal. To ask for the list: ¿Me trae la carta, por favor?

", "

Talking to the waiter: usted

English has one “you” for everyone. Spanish has a polite “you,” usted, which takes the third person singular, as if you were talking about “him” or “her” (a bit like an old-fashioned “Would sir like…?”). For several people, it's ustedes with the third person plural.

tú (friend, young waiter)usted (polite)
traer (to bring)¿Me traes agua?¿Me trae agua?
recomendar (ie)¿Qué me recomiendas?¿Qué me recomienda?
poder¿Puedes traer la cuenta?¿Puede traer la cuenta?
tener¿Tienes mesa?¿Tiene mesa?

¿Me trae…? (could you bring me…?) comes from traer, which is irregular in the first person (traigo) but regular in the third: trae. Learn it as a set phrase, like me pone at the market.

To…You say
ask for a table¿Tienen mesa para dos? (you're addressing the whole restaurant: ustedes)
ask for a recommendation¿Qué me recomienda?
ask for something¿Me trae un poco de pan, por favor?
ask for the checkLa cuenta, por favor. / ¿Nos trae la cuenta?

In Spain, people are on informal terms a lot, even in bars: a young waiter will often say ¿Qué quieres? to you. In a more traditional restaurant or with an older person, usted is still the right choice. In Latin America, ustedes replaces vosotros in every situation.

Buenas noches. ¿Tienen mesa para cuatro?Good evening. Do you have a table for four?
", "

Tapas, raciones and mealtimes

SpanishWhat it is
una tapaa small plate to go with a drink; in some cities (Granada, León), it comes free with your drink
una media racióna half portion, for tasting
una racióna full portion to share in the middle of the table
una cañaa small glass of draft beer
el aperitivoa drink and a tapa before the meal, around 1 p.m.

Quantities come back here: una ración de calamares, una botella de vino, un vaso de agua, un poco de pan.

Mealtimes

  • La comida (lunch): roughly 2 p.m. to 4 p.m.
  • La cena (dinner): from 9 p.m., often later on weekends.
  • At 7 p.m., lots of kitchens are closed: that's tapas time.

The check and tipping

You have to ask for la cuenta: the waiter won't bring it until you do. La propina (the tip) isn't expected the way it is in the US; people leave a little change if they're happy. Among friends, you'll often hear pagamos a medias (let's split it) or invito yo (it's on me).

Una ración de calamares y dos cañas, por favor.A portion of calamari and two draft beers, please.
